title: Never Stop Driving #198: The Next Epidemic
summary: When it comes to joining two wires, do you favor the solder joint or a crimp connector? That was the subject of a debate I incited in pit row last weekend. Yes, that is really how I choose to spend my time and I love every minute of it. The topic came up between races […]
body_markdown:
When it comes to joining two wires, do you favor the solder joint or a crimp connector? That was the subject of a debate I incited in pit row last weekend. Yes, that is really how I choose to spend my time and I love every minute of it.


The topic came up between races at our local track,[Waterford Hills](https://www.waterfordhills.com/) . Waterford, scene to generations of competition in SCCA (Sports Car Club of America) and other amateur series, hosts not just races but track days, driving schools, and other events on its 1.5-mile road course. It’s a gem and one of the finest places in the Midwest to commune with cars and car people.


Cameron Neveu


I was there with my two sons since we all compete in[Spec Racer Fords](https://scca-e.com/spec-racer-ford/) . These fiberglass-bodied, single-seat, open-cockpit formula cars with open wheels are the mainstay of SCCA amateur racing, because they’ve been around for ages, are readily available, and create a level playing field due to a standardized powertrain. The engine is a 1.9-liter Ford unit that powered Escort economy cars some 35 years ago.


Last weekend, my car was randomly dying on the track, forcing me to coast to a stop. I quickly figured out that simply cycling the ignition switch brought the car back to life. The car did the same thing a few more times, and I became a moving hazard: Imagine a tight group of cars at speed, and one in the middle suddenly slows, causing a pileup. Luckily, I made it to the pits before that happened.


I had the worst kind of electrical problem, an intermittent one that I could not replicate in the pits no matter how many wires and connections I shook. So, I threw parts at it, replacing the fuel-pump relay, the ignition switch, and even the fuel pump itself. Often in those situations, just poking around reveals something. For example, I was reasonably sure the crusty ignition switch was the smoking gun—Lord knows how old it was. For one race after I replaced that switch, the car ran perfectly. Problem solved! Alas, the issue returned before the day was done.


Cameron Neveu


The paddock of any amateur race is filled with DIY mechanics, who converged to offer advice. Discussion quickly shifted to the problems with vintage electronics. My car, despite its age, is computer-controlled.


A little silver box called the engine control unit (ECU) reads a variety of inputs and in return operates the fuel pump, the fuel injection, and the ignition. Electronic fuel injection, or[EFI](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/ecu-and-efi-101-a-beginners-guide-to-performance-tuning/) , introduced in the 1980s, is why modern cars now immediately start on cold mornings and emit far fewer harmful gases. Trouble is, like everything else, electronics degrade over time and can cause all manner of mysterious symptoms. The next fix to try for my car, for example, is a different ECU. The plastics that hold the computer chips oxidize and get brittle, which sometimes create micro-cracks that can create open circuits when they heat up. Maybe mine’s gone bad. There’s no way a DIYer can eyeball it and know.


Cameron Neveu


To be clear, I’m relaying hearsay here. The fun of being at Waterford is that a lot of the folks wandering the pits are genuine experts who work for car companies and suppliers. What we got to talking about is how the next wave of vintage cars, the ones from the ‘80s and ‘90s, all had some form of electronic control, making them susceptible to mysterious electronic maladies that can be very hard to track down.


The problem is not just the computers and the sensors. Even a 30-year-old car has a wiring harness that’s a bundle of[over a dozen insulated wires](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/what-you-need-to-know-about-automotive-wiring/) . The insulation breaks down over time, or moisture creeps into the wiring and corrodes from the inside out. My issue could simply be an old harness.


As we stood there in the pits, one of those Motown experts, Bosch chassis control engineer Vaughn Scott, drove up in his Porsche 924 Turbo and popped the hood. He’d replaced the Porsche’s stock fuel injection with an aftermarket system called[Microsquirt](https://diyautotune.com/products/microsquirt?srsltid=AfmBOop3VBAFjZ2yA3KSAgPFasezCE0hstwLt9Ffmou0DwKlCW36cAII) . For about $400, Microsquirt comes with the computer, engine wiring harness, and programming software.


Scott maintains that replacing old electronics is too logical to ignore. Once symptoms of aging electronics manifest, they tend to accelerate and are often extremely difficult to track down. Furthermore, new systems are far more capable and offer features like laptop communication. This is not a new debate; just recently, my colleague Kyle Smith[installed a Holley EFI system in his C4-generation Corvette.](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/fuel-injection-for-dummies-could-save-my-driving-season/)


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


For popular cars like Corvettes and Mustangs, companies like Holley offer what’s called “plug in play” systems, but for oddballs like Scott’s 924, you have to connect the new wiring harness to the existing sensors. That’s when we started talking about solder versus crimp. Scott claimed that installing Microsquirt is very doable for a do-it-yourselfer like me, but he’s a Bosch engineer with decades of experience. I seem to make problems worse as often as I fix them.


Regardless, I might be forced to heed Scott’s advice, because the electronics have gone haywire in a 1994 Ford Escort Cosworth RS I bought six months ago. There’s now a mysterious 4000-rpm rev limit, the ECU has gone into limp mode, and I can’t get into that brain and find out why. The “Cossie,” as it’s popularly known, was never sold here but has a cult following in England, so I’ve contacted numerous UK shops for help. On their advice, I’ve tested or replaced every sensor on the engine, yet the rev limit remains. The next step is to find out what’s going on in the ECU, but that will require me to ship the unit to England and have a shop install a $600 communication port. Then I might or might not be able to learn what’s causing the 4000-rpm rev limit.


The $600 is halfway to the cost of the Megasquirt ECU and wiring harness I’d need for the Ford. Do I spend on old tech, or look to the future? Even the UK shops that would modify the existing computer have said it’d be wiser to just replace the entire fuel-injection system for all the reasons Scott explained. I’m nervous to take on such a project—the user manual runs 327 pages!—but winter is coming, and I need something to do while I hide from the cold.


Cameron Neveu


Sometimes I pine for the good old days before fuel injection, but carbureted cars have their own problems. Remember that[Ferrari Dino I restored](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/dino-finito-hdc-dino-final-update-tktk/) over four years? I took it out the other night, and it started bucking and snorting and had no power. I immediately knew the problem since the same thing occurred a few months ago: A condenser had gone bad.[The condenser](https://www.hagerty.com/media/advice/piston-slap/piston-slap-of-condensers-and-resistors/) , a small metal tube about the size of a double-A battery, is basically an electrical damper that’s part of the ignition system. Like the more modern electronics, you can’t look at a condenser and see that it is bad, you just replace it. And today, the replacements are junk—I’ve replaced two in the past year.


The irony is not lost on me. We romanticize the simplicity of old cars, yet here I am chasing ghosts through three decades of increasingly complicated electronics across three very different machines. Is a new and modern EFI system the solution? It might be, and I must admit that after two years of fiddling with the Weber carburetors on the Ferrari, I’m tempted to switch to fuel injection since there’s a kit for it. Before I take that optional leap, however, it looks like I’ll have to upgrade the Cosworth ECU if I want to rev the Ford’s motor past four grand (I do). If nothing else, someone like me who tinkers with cars should get comfortable with these systems. If you have advice, I’m all ears!


While I’m considering my EFI future, let me share recent Hagerty Media material that knocked my socks off:

Larry
